claim: KtrAB from Vibrio alginolyticus binds ADP with a Kd of 3 μM.
source: integrated injection heat pulses, normalized per mole of injection, reveal differential binding curves calculated by a one-site binding model with determined Kd values of 3 μM for ADP and 2 μM for ATP.
evidence: The claim is supported by isothermal titration calorimetry data shown in Figure 2, which provides experimental measurements of binding affinity.

claim: KtrAB from Vibrio alginolyticus binds ATP with a Kd of 2 μM.
source: integrated injection heat pulses, normalized per mole of injection, reveal differential binding curves calculated by a one-site binding model with determined Kd values of 3 μM for ADP and 2 μM for ATP.
evidence: The claim is supported by isothermal titration calorimetry data shown in Figure 2, which provides experimental measurements of binding affinity.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of ADP-bound KtrAB was determined at an overall resolution of 6.6 Å.
source: A total of 20,500 particle images of ADP-bound KtrAB were combined to generate a cryo-EM map at an overall resolution of 6.6 Å with D2 symmetry imposed (Figures 3A and 4).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by cryo-EM data collection and processing described in the manuscript.

claim: The KtrAB complex has a KtrB2A8B2 composition.
source: The density map displays an octameric ring of KtrAs, associated on both sides with a KtrB dimer in a detergent belt (Figure 3A,B). This KtrB2A8B2 composition was confirmed by negative stain EM of the detergent-solubilized complex and native mass spectrometry (Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental techniques including cryo-EM, negative stain EM, and native mass spectrometry.

claim: The C-terminal domains of KtrA (C lobes) are poorly resolved in the cryo-EM map, indicating increased flexibility.
source: The C-terminal domains of KtrA, the so-called C lobes at the periphery of the KtrA ring, are poorly resolved, indicating an increased flexibility of these areas (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is based on the observation of poor resolution in specific regions of the cryo-EM density map.

claim: The KtrA ring has an oval shape in the ADP-bound state.
source: The KtrA ring has an oval shape (Figure 5C), as has been described for the homologous proteins within the complex (Cao et al., 2013), as well as for the solitary KtrA ring in the presence of ADP (Albright et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data from the current study and corroborated by previous structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: An elongated density protruding from each KtrB monomer into the octameric KtrA ring is observed in the ADP-bound KtrAB structure.
source: A remarkable feature of the KtrAB map, which has not previously been observed, is an elongated density protruding from each KtrB monomer into the octameric KtrA ring (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is based on direct observation of the cryo-EM density map.

claim: No densities are visible for D1M2b and the tip helix in the ADP-bound structure.
source: In contrast, no densities are visible for D1M2b and the tip helix, which form a helix hairpin at the membrane surface in the ATP-bound structure (cf. Figure 5A,B), suggesting large nucleotide-dependent conformational changes in this region.
evidence: The claim is based on the absence of density in the cryo-EM map and comparison with the ATP-bound structure.

claim: A subunit-interconnecting helix, 58 Å in length, spans the entire membrane and protrudes into the KtrA ring in the ADP-bound KtrAB model.
source: The most prominent feature in the ADP-bound KtrAB model is a subunit-interconnecting helix, 58 Å in length, which spans the entire membrane and protrudes into the KtrA ring (Figures 3C and 5A).
evidence: The claim is based on the structural model fitted into the cryo-EM density map.

claim: Helix D1M2 is extended by approximately 30 Å in the ADP-bound conformation compared to the ATP-bound structure.
source: This helix is an extension of helix D1M2, which in the ATP-bound structure is ~28 Å long.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of structural models in different nucleotide-bound states.

claim: Helix D4M2b is extended by 18 Å (3.3 helical turns) in the ADP-bound conformation compared to the ATP-bound state.
source: The adjacent C-terminal helix D4M2b is extended by 18 Å (3.3 helical turns) in the ADP-bound conformation compared to the ATP-bound state and also spans the entire membrane (cf. Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of structural models in different nucleotide-bound states.

claim: The major conformational changes in D1M2 and D4M2 narrow the pores in the ADP-bound conformation.
source: These major conformational changes in D1M2 and D4M2 together obviously narrow the pores in the ADP-bound conformation (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The claim is based on structural comparison and inference from the observed conformational changes.

claim: In the ADP-bound conformation, D1M2 forms one continuous, elongated α-helix that reaches into the octameric KtrA ring.
source: In the ADP-bound conformation, D1M2 forms one continuous, elongated α-helix that reaches into the octameric KtrA ring, probably enabling direct interactions with nearby residues close to the ADP-binding sites (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is based on the structural model and includes speculation about functional interactions.

claim: The extended α-helix of D1M2 is unlikely to form in the presence of ATP due to steric hindrance.
source: An overlay of the KtrB subunits in the ADP-bound state and the KtrA ring in its ATP-bound conformation implies that this extended α-helix is unlikely to form in the presence of ATP, due to steric hindrance (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is based on structural modeling and inference from steric considerations.

claim: In the ATP-bound conformation, D1M2 is twice broken, forming a short transmembrane α-helix with a C-terminal helix hairpin extending to the cytoplasmic membrane surface.
source: In the crystallized ATP-bound conformation, D1M2 is twice broken, forming a short transmembrane α-helix with a C-terminal helix hairpin extending to the cytoplasmic membrane surface (Figures 5B and 6B).
evidence: The claim is based on previously published crystal structures cited in the manuscript.

claim: ATP interacts with two different KtrAs via its γ-phosphate group, whereas ADP interaction occurs within one subunit.
source: The ADP- and ATP-bound structural models (Cao et al., 2013; Vieira-Pires et al., 2013) reveal that ATP interacts with two different KtrAs via its γ-phosphate group, whereas ADP interaction occurs within one subunit.
evidence: The claim is based on previously published structural models.

claim: The disparate interactions of nucleotides allow the diamond-shaped conformation of the RCK domain in the ADP-bound state, whereas the square-shaped ATP-bound state excludes the straightening of the α-helix by steric hindrance.
source: These disparate interactions of the nucleotides allow the diamond-shaped conformation of the RCK domain in the ADP-bound state in presence of the elongated D1M2 helix, whereas the square-shaped ATP-bound state excludes the straightening of the α-helix by steric hindrance (cf. Figure 5C,D).
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis and inference about the relationship between nucleotide binding and conformational states.

claim: Pulsed EPR measurements on spin-labeled KtrAB A122CR1 show a broad distance distribution in the range of 2 to 5 nm in the presence of ADP.
source: Indeed, the slow decline of the dipolar evolution functions in the presence of ATP indicates long distances, which according to the Tikhonov regularization center around 5.3 nm (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 3). The shift to longer distances becomes more pronounced with increasing ATP concentrations. In analogy to the measurements in the presence of ATP, the experimentally determined dipolar evolution functions in the presence of ADP show a fast decay with poor oscillations, which correspond to broad distance distributions centered around 3.0 nm (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by pulsed EPR spectroscopy data.

claim: Pulsed EPR measurements on spin-labeled KtrAB A122CR1 show distances centered around 5.3 nm in the presence of ATP.
source: Indeed, the slow decline of the dipolar evolution functions in the presence of ATP indicates long distances, which according to the Tikhonov regularization center around 5.3 nm (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by pulsed EPR spectroscopy data.

claim: The EPR measurements reflect the nucleotide-dependent conformational change of the D1M2 region between the formation of helix hairpins (in the presence of ATP) and elongated helix (in the presence of ADP).
source: In summary, the measurements reflect the nucleotide-dependent conformational change of the D1M2 region between the formation of the helix hairpins (in the presence of ATP) and elongated helix (in the presence of ADP).
evidence: The claim is based on interpretation of EPR data in the context of structural models.

claim: In the absence of nucleotides, the dipolar evolution function represents an intermediate between the ADP-bound and ATP-bound conformations.
source: In the absence of nucleotides, the dipolar evolution function represents an intermediate between the two functions in the presence of ADP and ATP, respectively. This results in a distance distribution between 2 and 6 nm, with an equal probability of contributions from both conformations (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by EPR data showing intermediate distance distributions.

claim: The molecular gate in KtrB is formed by the intramembrane loop located just below the selectivity filter and a highly conserved arginine residue (R427 in VaKtrAB) in D4M2.
source: The molecular gate in KtrB is thought to be formed by the intramembrane loop located just below the selectivity filter and a highly conserved arginine residue (R427 in VaKtrAB) in D4M2 situated in the same plane (Figure 6A,B and Figure 1C) (Cao et al., 2011, 2013; Hänelt et al., 2010a, 2010b).
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis and previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: The kinks in α-helices D1M2 and D4M2 introduced by the conformational change from the ADP- to the ATP-bound state are located in the gating region.
source: Interestingly, also the kinks in α-helices D1M2 and D4M2 introduced by the conformational change from the ADP- to the ATP-bound state are located in this region (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: The claim is based on structural comparison between ADP- and ATP-bound states.

claim: The kink in D4M2 may directly reorient the gating arginine residue (R427) and move it away from the intramembrane loop.
source: The kink in D4M2 may even directly reorient the gating arginine residue (R427) and move it away from the intramembrane loop as it is contained within the altered part of D4M2.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on structural inference.

claim: The proposed gating region is marked by a glycine-rich ring.
source: Remarkably, the proposed gating region is also marked by a glycine-rich ring (Figure 1C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), which in other K+ channels is linked to the gating region and is referred to as glycine hinge (Jiang et al., 2002a).
evidence: The claim is based on structural observation and comparison with other K+ channels.

claim: MD simulations demonstrate that in the ADP-bound conformation, α-helices D1M2 and D4M2 interact with the gating motifs in KtrB and hinder water accessibility.
source: However, the resolution of our density map is not high enough to draw detailed conclusions on the conformation of the gate. Instead, MD simulations demonstrate that in the ADP-bound conformation, α-helices D1M2 and D4M2 interact with the gating motifs in KtrB and hinder water accessibility.
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: In the presence of ATP, the number of water molecules in the cavity below the gating region increases due to the discontinuous structure of D1M2 and D4M2.
source: In the presence of ATP, the number of water molecules in the cavity below the gating region increases due to the discontinuous structure of D1M2 and D4M2, making the gate accessible to water from the cytoplasmic side (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: The conformation of the intramembrane loop has a minimal effect on the hydration level of the gating region.
source: Results for the water accessibility in the ADP- and ATP-bound states agree with those of the original simulations. Within the model uncertainties, the conformation of the loop thus has a minimal effect on the hydration level of the gating region (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by additional MD simulations with blindly modeled intramembrane loops.

claim: The water accessibility of the gating region is mainly dependent on the D1M2 and D4M2 conformations.
source: Therefore, the water accessibility of the gating region is mainly dependent on the D1M2 and D4M2 conformations.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from MD simulation results.

claim: In the absence of KtrA subunits, the intermolecular distances between residues T318CR1 in the KtrB dimer display a broad distance distribution both in the absence and presence of a K+ gradient.
source: In the absence of the KtrA subunits, the intermolecular distances between residues T318CR1 in the KtrB dimer display a broad distance distribution both in the absence and presence of the K+ gradient (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A), indicating the high flexibility of the intramembrane loop independent of a K+ gradient.
evidence: The claim is supported by pulsed EPR measurements on KtrB alone.

claim: In the presence of KtrA and ADP inside liposomes, the intramembrane loop is immobilized, showing a narrow distance distribution centered around 3.3 nm.
source: In contrast, in the presence of KtrA and upon the inclusion of ADP inside the liposomal lumen, the recorded pulsed EPR spectrum shows a defined oscillation, which marks a narrow distance distribution centered around 3.3 nm. This narrow distance distribution reflects the immobilization of the intramembrane loop (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by pulsed EPR measurements on reconstituted KtrAB.

claim: In the presence of ATP inside liposomes and external K+, the intramembrane loop shows a broader distance distribution and is shifted toward longer distances.
source: However, in the presence of ATP inside the liposomes and upon the external addition of K+, the oscillation of the spectrum becomes less defined, demonstrating a broader distance distribution and thus the movement of the intramembrane loop. Furthermore, the mean distance is shifted toward longer distances, suggesting an increased probability of an open conformation for facilitation of the flux of potassium ions (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by pulsed EPR measurements on reconstituted KtrAB.

claim: In the ADP-bound conformation of the KtrAB complex with elongated α-helices D1M2 and D4M2, the molecular gate is stabilized in its inactivated, closed conformation.
source: In summary, this set of measurements demonstrates that in the ADP-bound conformation of the KtrAB complex with its elongated α-helices D1M2 and D4M2, the molecular gate is stabilized in its inactivated, closed conformation.
evidence: The claim is based on interpretation of EPR data.

claim: The binding of ATP unlocks the intramembrane loop and enables the stochastic movement of the gate.
source: In contrast, the binding of ATP likely unlocks the intramembrane loop and enables the stochastic movement of the gate.
evidence: The claim is based on interpretation of EPR data and includes speculation about the mechanism.

claim: MD simulations on the KtrB subunit of the ATP-bound X-ray structure confirm the flexibility of the intramembrane loop in this conformation.
source: In fact, MD simulations on the KtrB subunit of the ATP-bound X-ray structure of KtrAB from B. subtilis (Vieira-Pires et al., 2013) confirm the flexibility of the intramembrane loop in this conformation (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: A K+ gradient, the surrounding membrane, and/or other factors are needed to stabilize the active, open conformation.
source: Finally, as supported by the comparison of samples in detergent solution and liposomes, a K+ gradient, the surrounding membrane and/or other factors yet to be identified are needed to stabilize the active, open conformation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparing EPR data in different experimental conditions.

claim: Under non-activating conditions, ADP is bound to the RCK subunits in a conformation with extended α-helices D1M2.
source: Our results lead us to the proposal of an activation mechanism: Under non-activating conditions, ADP is bound to the RCK subunits in a conformation with extended α-helices D1M2, which are stabilized by specific, not yet identified interactions between KtrA and KtrB similar to a spring tension state.
evidence: The claim is part of a proposed mechanism based on the structural and functional data presented.

claim: At the gating regions of KtrB, α-helices D1M2 and D4M2 probably form stable interactions with the conserved arginine residue and/or residues of the intramembrane loop, locking the gate in its rigid, closed conformation.
source: At the gating regions of KtrB α-helices D1M2 and D4M2 probably form stable interactions with the conserved arginine residue and/or residues of the intramembrane loop. These interactions lock the gate in its rigid, closed conformation.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on structural inference and the proposed mechanism.

claim: Upon a hyperosmotic shock, the internal ATP concentration increases.
source: Upon a hyperosmotic shock the internal ATP concentration increases (Ohwada and Sagisaka, 1987; Ohwada et al., 1994), which leads to the replacement of ADP by ATP in a competitive manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ATP binding induces the conformational change of the octameric KtrA ring resulting in the formation of helix hairpins of D1M2 at the membrane surface and partial unfolding of D4M2.
source: ATP binding then induces the conformational change of the octameric KtrA ring (Albright et al., 2006) resulting in the formation of helix hairpins of D1M2 at the membrane surface and partial unfolding of D4M2.
evidence: The claim is part of the proposed mechanism based on structural data and previous studies.

claim: In the activated state, the gating region is unlocked, enabling conformational changes of the intramembrane loop within the pore, which in principle allows K+ ions to translocate.
source: The protein is in its activated state; hence, the gating region is unlocked, enabling conformational changes of the intramembrane loop within the pore, which in principle allows K+ ions to translocate (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is part of the proposed mechanism based on the data presented.

claim: Patch-clamp measurements on TrkAH and whole-cell K+ uptake studies on KtrAB suggest prolonged opening probabilities in the presence of ATP.
source: However, instead of stochastic opening events which are enabled by the unlocking of the gating region, patch-clamp measurements on TrkAH (Cao et al., 2013) and whole-cell K+ uptake studies on KtrAB (Tholema et al., 1999) suggest prolonged opening probabilities in the presence of ATP, such that additional factors are required to stabilize the active, open state.
evidence: The claim is based on previous functional studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Lipids may play an essential role in the regulatory process of KtrAB.
source: Lipids, for instance, may play an essential role in the regulatory process and their role should be further investigated.
evidence: The claim is speculative, suggesting a potential role for lipids.

claim: Na+ ions have been previously described to activate the KtrAB system.
source: Furthermore, Na+ ions (Tholema et al., 1999) and protons (Stumpe et al., 1996) have been previously described to activate the KtrAB and TrkAH systems, respectively, but their molecular role is not yet understood.
evidence: The claim is based on previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Protons have been previously described to activate the TrkAH system.
source: Furthermore, Na+ ions (Tholema et al., 1999) and protons (Stumpe et al., 1996) have been previously described to activate the KtrAB and TrkAH systems, respectively, but their molecular role is not yet understood.
evidence: The claim is based on previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: A three-stage translocation mechanism has been suggested previously for a variety of different single-pore RCK channels.
source: A three-stage translocation mechanism has been suggested previously for a variety of different single-pore RCK channels (Hite et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2002b; Kong et al., 2012) (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is based on previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: The three-stage translocation mechanism implies that ligand-induced conformational changes in the RCK domain are transferred via a flexible linker to the helical bundle of the pore domain.
source: This translocation mechanism implies that ligand-induced conformational changes in the RCK domain are transferred via a flexible linker to the helical bundle of the pore domain.
evidence: The claim describes the previously proposed mechanism for other RCK channels.

claim: The data suggest an unexpected, new mechanism of regulation for the Ktr/Trk family.
source: Our data suggest an unexpected, new mechanism of regulation for the Ktr/Trk family.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement based on all the data presented in the study.

claim: The unique features of the Ktr/Trk family are the existence of two parallel pores and the non-covalent association of cytoplasmic RCK subunits.
source: The unique features of this family, namely the existence of two parallel pores and the non-covalent association of cytoplasmic RCK subunits require a modified regulation mechanism.
evidence: The claim is based on structural knowledge of the Ktr/Trk family.

claim: In the Ktr/Trk family, the functions of the flexible linker and the helical bundle are transferred to the movement of the elongated helices and their interactions with the gating regions.
source: The functions of the flexible linker and the helical bundle are transferred to the movement of the elongated helices and their interactions with the gating regions.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of the new mechanism with the previously known mechanism in other RCK channels.

claim: Ktr/Trk systems are key players for the homeostasis of bacterial cell physiology, encasing osmotic resistance, cellular fitness during host infection, and antimicrobial resistance.
source: Ktr/Trk systems are key players for the homeostasis of bacterial cell physiology, encasing osmotic resistance, cellular fitness during host infection (Alkhuder et al., 2010; Stingl et al., 2007) and antimicrobial resistance (Diskowski et al., 2015; Gries et al., 2013; Su et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Ktr/Trk systems are essential for bacteria but not present in mammalian cells.
source: Ktr/Trk systems are essential for bacteria but not present in mammalian cells.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the distribution of these systems.

claim: The newly discovered inactive conformation may be a suitable target for structure-guided drug development of an entirely new line of antibiotics.
source: Therefore, the newly discovered inactive conformation may be a suitable target for structure-guided drug development of an entirely new line of antibiotics.
evidence: The claim is speculative, suggesting potential applications of the findings.

claim: K+ concentration within the cell is responsible for pH homeostasis, cell growth, maintenance of osmolarity and cell volume, movement and electrical signaling.
source: Within the cell, the K+ concentration is responsible for a plethora of tasks, including pH homeostasis (Bakker and Mangerich, 1981; Kroll and Booth, 1981; Plack and Rosen, 1980), cell growth, maintenance of osmolarity and cell volume (Schultz et al., 1963), movement and electrical signaling (Hille, 2001).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge and previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: The majority of prokaryotic ligand-gated K+ channels and many eukaryotic systems consist of a single tetrameric pore regulated by covalently linked cytoplasmic ligand-binding domains termed RCK.
source: The majority of the prokaryotic ligand-gated K+ channels and many eukaryotic systems consist of a single tetrameric pore regulated by covalently linked cytoplasmic ligand-binding domains, termed regulator of K+ conductance (RCK) (Jiang et al., 2001, 2002b).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge and previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: A three-stage regulatory mechanism via the RCK domains has been proposed for various K+ uptake systems.
source: Based on the structural knowledge of various K+ uptake systems, a three-stage regulatory mechanism via the RCK domains has been proposed (Chakrapani and Perozo, 2007; Hite et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2002a, 2002b; Ye et al., 2006; Yuan et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: The pore subunits (KtrB/TrkH) of the osmoprotective systems Ktr and Trk merely interact with the cytoplasmic RCK subunits (KtrA/TrkA), missing the covalent helical linkage.
source: In contrast to the aforementioned K+ channels, the pore subunits (KtrB/TrkH) of the osmoprotective systems Ktr and Trk merely interact with the cytoplasmic RCK subunits (KtrA/TrkA), missing the covalent helical linkage (Cao et al., 2013; Vieira-Pires et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on previous structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Instead of a single pore, two neighboring pores are regulated by one octameric ring of RCK subunits in Ktr and Trk systems.
source: Furthermore, instead of a single pore, two neighboring pores are regulated by one octameric ring of RCK subunits (Albright et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is based on previous structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Ktr and Trk systems exhibit a very similar structure.
source: Ktr and Trk systems exhibit a very similar structure.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about these systems.

claim: Each KtrB and TrkH monomer consists of four pairs of covalently linked transmembrane helices (D1-D4) that surround the ion pathway and together constitute the pore.
source: Each KtrB and TrkH monomer consists of four pairs of covalently linked transmembrane helices (D1-D4) that surround the ion pathway and together constitute the pore (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is based on structural knowledge and previous studies.

claim: The two transmembrane helices M1 and M2 of each repeat are joined by pore loops (P loops), which form the selectivity filter.
source: The two transmembrane helices M1 and M2 of each repeat are joined by pore loops (P loops), which form the selectivity filter (Cao et al., 2013; Durell and Guy, 1999; Vieira-Pires et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on structural knowledge and previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: The selectivity filter of KtrB and TrkH is less conserved compared to the TVGYG motif of classical K+ channels.
source: Compared to the TVGYG motif of classical K+ channels, the selectivity filter of KtrB and TrkH is less conserved (Zhou et al., 2001); a single glycine residue of each of the four P loops converges within the ion pathway (Figure 1) (Tholema et al., 1999, 2005).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence comparison and previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: An intramembrane loop formed by the central part of broken D3M2 directly beneath the selectivity filter represents a unique structural motif that regulates K+ flow by blocking and opening of the pore.
source: An intramembrane loop formed by the central part of broken D3M2 directly beneath the selectivity filter represents a unique structural motif that regulates K+ flow by blocking and opening of the pore.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis and previous functional studies.

claim: The intramembrane loop together with a highly conserved arginine residue in D4M2 forms the molecular gate.
source: The intramembrane loop (Hänelt et al., 2010a, 2010b) together with a highly conserved arginine residue in D4M2 (Cao et al., 2011) forms the molecular gate (cf. Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is based on previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Regulation of the pore subunits, KtrB and TrkH, is thought to occur via nucleotide-dependent conformational changes of the octameric RCK subunits.
source: Regulation of the pore subunits, KtrB and TrkH, is thought to occur via nucleotide-dependent conformational changes of the octameric RCK subunits (Cao et al., 2013; Kröning et al., 2007; Szollosi et al., 2016; Vieira-Pires et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: X-ray structures revealed distinct ATP- or ADP-induced conformational changes within the RCK ring, whereas the pore conformation was almost identical.
source: X-ray structures revealed distinct ATP- or ADP-induced conformational changes within the RCK ring, whereas the pore conformation was almost identical (Szollosi et al., 2016; Vieira-Pires et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on previous structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: The link between conformational changes within the RCK subunits and pore permeability remained elusive prior to this study.
source: However, the link between conformational changes within the RCK subunits and pore permeability remained elusive.
evidence: The claim identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: The KtrB2A8B2 assembly is probably formed during protein purification due to the symmetry of the octameric KtrA ring, which has identical binding sites for the KtrB dimer on both sides.
source: This assembly, also observed in crystal structures of KtrAB and TrkAH homologs (Cao et al., 2013; Vieira-Pires et al., 2013), is probably formed during protein purification due to the symmetry of the octameric KtrA ring, which has identical binding sites for the KtrB dimer on both sides.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from structural observations and previous studies.

claim: The density cross-correlation coefficient improved from 0.70 in the initial model to 0.89 after MDFF simulation.
source: The density cross-correlation coefficient, used as fit quality indicator, improved from 0.70 in the initial model to 0.89.
evidence: The claim is based on computational modeling data.

claim: The KtrAB variant A122C is functional as confirmed by growth complementation assay.
source: The functionality of the mutant was confirmed by a growth complementation assay at limiting K+ concentrations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional assay data.

claim: The KtrAB variant T318C is functional as confirmed by growth complementation assay.
source: The mutants' functionality again was confirmed using the complementation assay (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional assay data.

claim: Recent data suggest another level of regulation by the binding of cyclic nucleotides to the C lobes of KtrA.
source: Additionally, recent data suggest another level of regulation by the binding of cyclic nucleotides to the C lobes of KtrA, which likely plays an additional role for the inactivation of the system (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on a recent study cited in the manuscript.

claim: The lipid composition is adjusted upon a hyperosmotic shock.
source: This hypothesis seems plausible knowing that the lipid composition is adjusted upon a hyperosmotic shock (Romantsov et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on a previous study cited in the manuscript.

claim: Compatible solute transporters were shown to be activated by altered lipid composition.
source: The deactivation of the KtrAB system might be coordinated with the activation of compatible solute transporters, which were shown to be activated by the altered lipid composition (Culham et al., 2003; Peter et al., 1996; Rübenhagen et al., 2000; Schiller et al., 2006; van der Heide et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is based on previous studies cited in the manuscript.
